doc.title: Ray Shiner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 1998

title: A concert band booked as a dance band; confusion with Ralph Flanagan
summary: Wrong agent, puzzled dance audiences, college dates, and RCA confusing Finegan with Flanagan.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Okay. That the big band era—
Yeah. These guys wanted to do it anyway.

Yeah. They had the wrong booking agent, Willard Alexander, who was used to booking dance bands, and we were not a dance band, we were a concert band for listening. You could dance to us, because Eddie and Bill wrote arrangements which were conducive to dancing, but it was very puzzling to the audience because the melody used to shift from one section to the next or a different combination of instruments. We’d get to a gig and the people would yell up to the bandstand, “Why don’t you play something we can dance to?” And Sonny Russo, my roommate on the band would yell down, “Why don’t you dance to something we can play to?” It was a very funny band too. We all had a great sense of humor and we had a hundred percent backing from the leaders.
Yeah? Did they play with the band also?

Well Eddie loved to — he was a frustrated percussion player. And Finegan just directed, well he was a great piano player. They were both consummate musicians and we adored them. Every night after the gig we’d walk up to them and apologize for the mistakes we made in the arrangements.
So what would a tour at that time consist of for you? Was it playing colleges or dance halls?

It was playing a lot of colleges. Originally we played every dance hall in the eastern circuit, which was a certain death. You know, people, they didn’t understand our band or know what we were playing, didn’t know what we were doing or they could care even less.
I’m trying to place the pop music that was going on in the early ‘50s too. It wasn’t quite rock & roll yet.

Well they confused us with Ralph Flanagan, that’s probably the biggest insult you could give us because Ralph Flanagan to us was the lowest. But some idiot at RCA confused the name Flanagan with Finegan.
And stuck with it, and insisted Ralph Flanagan was the band, because he thought it was Bill Finegan. He had the names confused.
So he was promoting the group as a sound that didn’t exist.
